title: Museum of Soviet Arcade Machines
text:
The museum was founded in 2007 by graduates of the Moscow Polytechnic University Alexander Stakhanov, Alexander Vugman and Maxim Pinigin and was located in the basement-bomb shelter of the university dormitory.[1] At that time, the museum's collection included 37 arcade machines. It was possible to visit the museum only on Wednesdays and by prior arrangement.[2]

> It all started when we wanted to have the "Sea Battle" arcade machine at home, and we realized that it was interesting not only for us, but also for our friends. — Alexander Stakhanov [3]

The founders of the museum looked for the first arcade machines all over the country in landfills, abandoned pioneer camps, parks, cultural centers and cinemas. Several machines, which were the first in the collection, were bought for 210 rubles in the park of Pryamikov on Taganka. However, the dream of the "Sea Battle" was never realized, since the arcade machines were incomplete. Almost all the machines that came to the museum were not working, and one machine was assembled from three broken ones.[4,5]

In April 2010, the museum moved to the building of the former workshop of the Rot Front factory in Malaya Ordynka. The museum started to work daily, and the collection expanded to 40 kinds of arcade machines.[6]

In August 2011 the museum moved to Baumanskaya street, and the exposition was replenished with dozens of arcade machines.[7]

A branch of the museum was opened on June 15, 2013 on Koniushennaya Square in St. Petersburg.[8] It is located in a building that was used to store carriages in the 18th century. Garages, repair and production workshops of the Leningrad taxi fleet #1 were located on this territory during the Soviet times. The branch collection includes more than 50 working arcade machines.[9] According to the museum, the number of visitors to the St. Petersburg branch in 2016 totalled 23 000 people, which is 9% more than in 2015.[10]

At the end of August 2014, the third branch of the museum was opened in Kazan on the Kremlin street. About 40 arcade machines were presented there.[11] The museum did not exist for a long time — on January 12, 2015 it was closed.[12]

Since June 2015, the Moscow Museum of Soviet arcade machines is located on Kuznetsky Most Street. The museum's collection includes about 80 slot machines.[13]

In April 2017, the museum turned 10 years old.[5]
